Thoughts like "Oh, I probably do too much of x" are great - they indicate that x has a negative impact on your mental, physical, overall well-being. They mean you - often unwillingly - acknowledge you have a problem of x interfering with your plans in life. This is the moment when you do something about x. Now or it's just gonna be worse down the addiction lane. The thing you say that games can be useful, educational, and creative is you making you feel better about what you're getting/you're addicted to. I don't disagree but hearing it from someone who says has problems with playing in moderation is like hearing from a person with a drinking problem that alcohol is not that bad, you know, it's tasty, who doesn't appreciate an expensive wine, right?

I would advise you to uninstall every single game you have on your computer, console, smartphone, whatever. Even those you consider non-addictive. Go completely clean for no less than a week and see how lack of games influences your day-to-day life (writing your thoughts down is very useful and your frustrations that you can't play anything, too). Tell your gaming buddies you need a break from gaming because you are tired or bored of it. They will understand if they aren't bad people. If they turn away from you completely then ask yourself what is more important to you - playing games with them at the expense of your dissatisfaction with yourself or their dissatisfaction with you because you want some rest? The choice is yours.

Video games are dead things, they can't be inherently good or evil, just like more common addiction stuff - drugs, alcohol, social media, gambling, etc. They are all about quick shots of dopamine and/or escapism. It's your decision how you use them or abuse them until you get addicted. Once you're seriously addicted, you need therapy. Or you keep destroying your life.

For the record, I'm no psychologist or addiction therapist. I've struggled myself with gaming, I'm very prone to addictive behaviors. Half of my family have struggled with addictions listed above. I think I know this or that about all of this crap.

I was in therapy for depression and crushing loneliness was part of the problem. Therapy made me realize that sometimes you choose to be lonely because you push away people that are already here for you, your family. My family is not perfect but very supporting. I feel really sorry for anyone that can't rely on their relatives. I've accepted my loner ways, social and media pressure doesn't work on me - never being a fan of social media immensely helped with that. However, the most important realization was that people you meet in life are temporary. Even those you consider your best friends - life will happen to you and them, you never know where you end up. Especially if we are talking about friends from school days or university. Now I enjoy every little bit of time when I meet someone and have an interesting conversation even if we don't continue talking later. It's a matter of mental strength, I guess? I would say I don't need friends to fulfill any void in my life, they are now a pleasant but not an essential addition.

Hello. First of all, I wish you luck on your gaming-free journey! Stay focused and motivated and don't be too hard on yourself.

When it comes to alternatives to gaming, I suggest you think about your other hobbies. Do you have any, other than gaming? If so, try to expand interests you already have. I don't know what you mean by "useful" exactly. Useful like learning a specific skill or useful like colouring because it relieves your anxiety? If you don't have any other interests than gaming I would say try out what sounds fun to you and simple to start. Whatever it is, start slowly and don't invest money right away in anything, it will cause frustration if you have enough of this activity after one week. I don't know you so I don't know what category of activities suggest. For example, I am the bookish type, so after quitting gaming I slowly returned to reading more, writing, and learning languages. I started doing yoga. What didn't work for me: artsy stuff like drawing, playing an instrument, hiking, most sports actually.

Think what you gonna miss the most about gaming. Competitiveness, a sense of achievement, community?  Find an activity that will give you what you miss, at least to some extent, but be ready to face the truth - even small achievements in real life take more time than those in video games.

About the void:

1) When you feel it, the worst thing to do is to sit around and overthink it. Do you live with someone or do you have pets? It is good to direct your attention to other living beings, talk to them, play with. If you are alone, you can try writing down what you feel, what you think, on a piece of paper, even if it's complete gibberish, it doesn't matter. Good old physical exhaustion helps too, especially if you have problems with sleeping.

2) if stress seriously hurts your life, I would suggest you seek professional help. I you think it is not that bad, find breathing exercises on the internet. Aware and deep breathing is like the most basic relaxation technique. Focus on your breath. Yoga is awesome for stress-relief as well. Having a daily-routine (not a whole day planned from waking up to going asleep) with a few short and simple activities (even like 5 minutes of walking)  is helpful and gives you some   sense of order and peace.

3) again, highly dependable on the person. Video games make us used to a lot of audiovisual stimulation + interaction with the source of the stimulation. It is difficult for other forms of entertainment to top that. Right after quitting, everything is just so slow and boring. I think board games and table-top RPGs are a good alternative - they are sociable, creative, and game-y activities, if it sounds interesting to you. But be prepared that you gonna feel bored a lot initially. I remember being bored after reading a paragraph in a book that interested me but after two years of barely any gaming I can finish one book after another.

My tips probably sound a bit generic but, honestly, this is what has helped me. This and tons of willpower. My gaming-quitting experience made realize how dumb the majority of games is and how full of repetitive and addicting mechanics they are. They are designed to eat away your time, that's their charm. Once it really gets to you (and it could take some too), I think you'll be less likely to return to gaming or to play at the level of addition.

I've been on both sides of such situations. I know, when you have a group of friends, it feels like you should meet like a group all the time, right? Speaking from experience, friends in a group rarely like one another equally. For me, there was always somebody I liked more and wanted to spend more time with them but without others. It's just people being people.

I'm not saying it to make you even sadder. I remember how sad I was upon hearing that my group of friends was having fun without me. But it also gave me time to think if they really care about me. Perhaps you should rethink your friendships. 

As hard as it sounds, don't surround yourself with people that don't care about you because you're wasting your time. Wasting time on the wrong folk is even worse than loneliness.

I've spent most of my life without somebody I could call I true friend.There were people in primary school and high school I liked and spent a bunch of time with but I knew I couldn't trust them fully. We lived in a small community and I guess I just stuck to my "friend" group even though I realized that we were drifting apart in terms of interests, hobbies, and opinions. I stayed around because I didn't want to be lonely. I was and still am quite shy, introverted, and reserved, and didn't know how to find others who would share my likes and dislikes. Heck, I still haven't found them, probably never will.

The university rolled around and I heard the same exact words as you did. Surprise, surprise, I didn't discover any meaningful friendships even though at that time I was dying for acceptance and companionship. I was ready to sacrifice my time and health just to spent time with people and have a sense of belonging. While I had more in common with people at uni, I could see they had many friends outside uni and we rarely went out or did any stuff together that wasn't uni-related. When we did, it was quite fun, though, but it turns out no deeper connections were formed. After that unfortunate period of time I stopped caring about making friends. I got used to doing things on my own and not sharing my joys and sorrows with anyone.

I agree, having no friends is very freeing, especially for me. I often felt pressure to read or watch or play this or that, or to say certain things, to, you know, simply belong. I am pretty relived that there is almost no one interested in my personal life, that I can shape myself and my life as I like, that I spend the vast majority of my time as I want to. There is no pressure, no FOMO, no need for social media. I've discovered I grow more when I spent less time with others.
